title: Understanding and Repairing Cooperative Perception under Adverse Weather
abstract: A cooperative detector can lose a correct vehicle detection when surrounding LiDAR measurements change, even if the returns on the vehicle remain unchanged. We study this failure as Weather-Induced Context Interference. On our CoInfra development set, controlled removal outside annotated object boxes turns 22.1% of V2X-ViT's previously correct detections into misses. Restoring network features around the objects to their values before removal recovers 98.6% of these misses. The same restoration in each of three equally sized regions excluding the objects recovers none. Candidate analysis finds accurate boxes that are not selected, while other targets lack well-localized candidates. With paired reference features unavailable at inference, Adverse-Weather Cooperative Repair (AWCR) repairs candidates from current observations. A lightweight Local Correction head generates bounded alternatives, and Quality Selection ranks them alongside original boxes with a correction weight. In V2X-R simulation, AWCR also filters peer returns before detection using Point Classifier trained on generated-point labels. Candidate repair improves mean car BEV AP@0.7 by 4.22 points across three fits on natural adverse-weather CoInfra development inputs and vehicle AP@0.7 by 5.00 points on a rain-affected public recording. It also improves released HEAL, FadeLead, and V2X-DGW detectors with their pretrained weights fixed. On the full V2X-Radar-C validation benchmark, HEAL with AWCR achieves state-of-the-art LiDAR-only cooperative detection performance of 68.22 vehicle BEV AP@0.7.

title: Zero-HLM: Generalizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation without Real Robot Data
abstract: Learning generalizable humanoid loco-manipulation remains bottlenecked by costly real-world demonstrations. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, but requires visually faithful, physics-ready scenes and executable whole-body motions. We present Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that transforms smartphone captures and simulated source demonstrations into scalable training data for humanoid loco-manipulation. Gaussian-guided agentic real-to-sim reconstruction aligns visual and physical scenes; motion-environment co-adaptation uses rollout feedback to correct whole-body references and interaction geometry. We generate 4,800 physically validated demonstrations for zero-shot transfer across three Unitree G1 tasks. Simulation-trained GR00T N1.7 achieves 66.7% mean full-task success, versus 46.7% with real-data training. On generalized configurations, expanded simulation training raises pooled success from 23% for base-trained real-data policies to 69%, without additional real demonstrations. Project page: https://young-bit.github.io/zero-hlm/

title: Scaling and Renormalization in Neural Networks: An Effective Renormalization-Group Description of Grokking
abstract: Grokking is a delayed transition from memorization to generalization in deep neural networks (NNs). We examine whether scaling and renormalization group (RG) theories can describe this dynamics, establishing a quantitative physical framework for neural generalization transitions. For modular addition on a two-layer NN, an ensemble of trained models defines an order parameter (the squared weight norm) and fluctuation proxies for the heat capacity and the susceptibility, with training epoch and weight decay serving as thermal and field control coordinates. To bridge neural architectures to real-space RG, we construct an exact coupling matrix via a second-order expansion of the loss with respect to per-neuron norms and use its Fiedler vector to define an effective geometry. This spectral ordering yields a monotonic spatial decay of coupling strength that is absent under random permutations. We then execute real-space RG by block-spin aggregating adjacent neurons and parameterizing the coupling matrix into off-diagonal band strengths. Linearizing this local RG map yields relevant scaling exponents and five derived critical exponents, with direct empirical estimates matching RG predictions within 1-10%. Overall, our framework provides a consistent effective description of grokking, suggesting the scaling and renormalization group formalism as a tool to investigate NN dynamics.

title: Proofs of strong forms of the Bovdi--Geche universality conjecture and a complex analogue
abstract: We prove two universality theorems for neural networks consisting of a single neuron. First we prove a strong form of the Bovdi--Geche universality conjecture on neurons over finite fields, where the activation function is a certain modification of the discrete logarithm, using the Weil bound on multiplicative character sums over finite fields. Then we show a generalisation of Aizenberg's universality theorem for complex binary neurons with a weight vector independent of the target function, positively answering another question in the literature. The proof of the latter uses an equidistribution theorem for the dilates of certain maps into tori.

title: Understanding the Co-evolutionary Solution Exchange of the MOEA/D: Already the Smallest Communication Radius Gives the Best-Possible Speed-Up
abstract: Besides domination-based algorithms such as the NSGA-II, the decomposition-based MOEA/D is one of the most popular and successful optimization heuristic for multi-objective problems. It decomposes the problem into several, single-objective subproblems. By solving these in a co-evolutionary manner and archiving non-dominated solutions, it approximates or computes the Pareto front. Interestingly, so far no advantages from the co-evolutionary communication of subproblem solutions were proven. In this first mathematical runtime analysis addressing this research question, we investigate how the mutation-based MOEA/D solves the classic OneMinMax benchmark when solutions are exchanged among subproblems in different distances $r$. We show, for the first time, that the MOEA/D profits from an exchange of solutions, and that already very small communication radii $r$ are sufficient to maximally profit from this feature of the algorithm. More precisely, for all values $r \ge 1$ we prove a tight runtime guarantee of $Θ(n^2)$, where $n$ is the problem size. This is asymptotically faster than the known bound of $O(n^2 \log n)$ guarantee for $r=0$, which we complement with a matching bound of $Ω(n^2 \log n)$.

title: FlowGenesis: Representation-Driven Self-Organization of Neural Architectures
abstract: Deep neural networks typically rely on architectures specified before training, despite the continuous evolution of their internal representations. We introduce FlowGenesis, a framework in which neural architectures adapt through neuron birth and pruning guided by Representation Flux, a local statistic capturing changes in minibatch mean activations. Neurons exhibiting persistently high Flux undergo splitting designed to approximately preserve the network function, while neurons with low Flux and low activity are pruned. This mechanism allows network capacity to evolve without prescribing a target architecture or performing a separate architecture search. Experiments on image and text classi- fication show that networks initialized with different sizes approach similar final neuron-count ranges within each dataset while maintaining comparable predictive performance. We further extend FlowGenesis to continual learning, where representation-guided structural adaptation reduces the neurons and parameters allocated to successive tasks while maintaining accuracy comparable to fixed-width Progressive Neural Networks in a task-incremental learning setting. These findings demonstrate that neural architectures can adapt through feedback between representation learning and structural change, suggesting an alternative to prescribing network capacity before training.

title: Priority-Preserving Advantage Aggregation for Multi-Reward Policy Optimization
abstract: LLM post-training often optimizes multiple objectives with unequal priorities, such as correctness and reasoning efficiency. However, the widely used additive reward aggregation in RL can violate these priorities: when primary and auxiliary advantages conflict, a sufficiently large auxiliary signal can overturn the preference induced by the primary objective. We term this problem \emph{advantage priority inversion}. Although reward-level gating can protect priority more directly, it still removes potentially useful auxiliary distinctions among rollout samples that fail the primary condition. To address this trade-off, we propose Primary Advantage Policy Optimization (\textbf{PAPO}), a priority-aware advantage aggregation method that asymmetrically combines a primary and an auxiliary advantage. PAPO retains auxiliary supervision when the objectives agree and smoothly attenuates conflicting auxiliary signals, preserving the primary sign during fusion for \emph{primary-consistent ordering}. This rule applies to sequence-level advantages in GRPO and token-level advantages in actor--critic PPO. Experiments on multiple domains and models show that PAPO consistently achieves the best primary objective while maintaining best or competitive auxiliary-objective performance across both GRPO- and PPO-based optimization. \href{https://xiangchi-yuan.github.io/papo-project/}{Code is available}.

title: LogicEye: Agent Driven Multimodal Dataset for Interpretable Ophthalmic Diagnosis
abstract: Clinical adoption of ophthalmic Artificial Intelligence remains limited by low interpretability and a lack of finely annotated multimodal data. Most existing datasets provide only coarse disease labels without the granular pathological findings required for differential diagnosis. We present LogicEye$^{Agent}$, a dual-pool inference and verification agent that emulates clinical reasoning by jointly verifying positive inclusion signs and negative exclusion criteria. Using LogicEye$^{Agent}$, we curate LogicEye$^{Data}$, a large-scale multimodal dataset of 804,461 fundus and OCT images paired with structured pathological reports spanning 38 diseases and 29 subtypes, with quality assured through joint verification by multimodal large language models and clinical experts. Building on this dataset, we further develop LogicEye$^{Bench}$, which incorporates a category-constrained loss for hierarchical disease recognition and report generation. Grounding coarse labels into verified visual findings effectively curtails diagnostic hallucinations and establishes a solid foundation for interpretable vision-language modeling in ophthalmology. The code is available at:https://github.com/Eden35/LogicEye-Agent-Driven-Multimodal-Dataset-for-Interpretable-Ophthalmic-Diagnosis.

title: Dirichlet Process Mixtures within Semiparametric Bayesian Networks: A Novel Conditional Density Estimation Approach
abstract: Semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBNs) are flexible probabilistic graphical models for representing joint distributions of continuous variables through lower-dimensional conditional probability distributions (CPDs). Existing SPBN models use kernel density estimators (KDEs) for non-parametric CPD modeling, but their one-component-per-observation mixture representation can lead to increased inference costs and density estimation errors, which can be limiting. In this work, we define a new CPD modeling approach for non-parametric components based on Bayesian non-parametric Dirichlet Process Mixtures (DPMs) within SPBNs. DPMs provide a data-adaptive clustering of observations, yielding a more compact representation while retaining the flexibility of non-parametric density estimation, unlike KDE. This results in lower inference costs while improving density estimation performance. We implement the proposed DPM-based SPBN (DPM-SPBN) by extending the open-source PyBNesian package and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world data. For a given network structure, DPM-based CPDs significantly outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian network models for continuous variables in density estimation, achieving lower absolute log-likelihood errors on synthetic data. We further investigate the impact of the proposed CPD modeling on structure learning methods relying on CPD-based scores. DPM-based SPBNs achieve lower structure learning and density estimation errors than KDE-based SPBNs. Experiments on real-world data corroborate these findings, identifying DPM-based CPD modeling as the most effective alternative among the evaluated non-parametric approaches for continuous variables.

evidence.title: Dirichlet Process Mixtures within Semiparametric Bayesian Networks: A Novel Conditional Density Estimation Approach
evidence.abstract: Semiparametric Bayesian networks (SPBNs) are flexible probabilistic graphical models for representing joint distributions of continuous variables through lower-dimensional conditional probability distributions (CPDs). Existing SPBN models use kernel density estimators (KDEs) for non-parametric CPD modeling, but their one-component-per-observation mixture representation can lead to increased inference costs and density estimation errors, which can be limiting. In this work, we define a new CPD modeling approach for non-parametric components based on Bayesian non-parametric Dirichlet Process Mixtures (DPMs) within SPBNs. DPMs provide a data-adaptive clustering of observations, yielding a more compact representation while retaining the flexibility of non-parametric density estimation, unlike KDE. This results in lower inference costs while improving density estimation performance. We implement the proposed DPM-based SPBN (DPM-SPBN) by extending the open-source PyBNesian package and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world data. For a given network structure, DPM-based CPDs significantly outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian network models for continuous variables in density estimation, achieving lower absolute log-likelihood errors on synthetic data. We further investigate the impact of the proposed CPD modeling on structure learning methods relying on CPD-based scores. DPM-based SPBNs achieve lower structure learning and density estimation errors than KDE-based SPBNs. Experiments on real-world data corroborate these findings, identifying DPM-based CPD modeling as the most effective alternative among the evaluated non-parametric approaches for continuous variables.

title: VPR-Space: A Benchmark for Visual Place Recognition in Space Analog Domains
abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$

title: Shared-Factor-Conditioned Diffusion for Low-Rank Tensor Recovery
abstract: Tensor recovery spans heterogeneous data structures and observation processes, calling for a representation that can adapt across modalities and tasks. We propose DiffTR, an unsupervised framework that unifies tensor completion, denoising, and hyperspectral super-resolution through coordinate-conditioned diffusion. Shared factors indexed by tensor coordinates condition a compact score network, and score matching jointly learns the factors and an implicit tensor representation from the available observations. Scalar and vector-valued outputs accommodate individual entries and entire tubes, enabling a common formulation for tabular tensors, images, and videos. The framework separates representation learning from task-specific observation modeling: reverse diffusion recovers missing values; estimation via Tweedie's formula, soft thresholding, and optional spatial consistency support mixed-noise denoising; and measurement-guided sampling transfers a prior learned from low-resolution hyperspectral observations to high-resolution reconstruction, followed by post-sampling refinement with data consistency and spectral subspace regularization. This separation makes the representation compatible with different corruption models and permits task-specific constraints to be incorporated within the same recovery framework. Experiments across multiple tensor modalities and recovery tasks demonstrate competitive reconstruction quality and the flexibility of a unified conditional generative representation. The code is available at https://github.com/CZY-Code/DiffTR

title: AgriDefend: A $205 Offline Edge Device that Detects Crop Stress Before Visible Symptoms via Multimodal AI Fusion
abstract: Most in-field crop-monitoring devices sense a single modality -- either a camera looking at the canopy or a probe reading the soil -- and so cannot detect stress that begins below ground before it becomes visible above it. We present AgriDefend, a self-contained consumer-grade edge device that fuses both. A MobileNetV2 convolutional neural network (CNN) analyses canopy imagery, and a Random Forest classifier integrates trend features from a single soil probe: moisture, the rate of change in pH and in N, P, K, and belowground CO2 relative to ambient (a proxy for soil respiration). A logistic-regression meta-learner fuses the two into a five-class crop-health prediction, all on a Raspberry Pi 5 with no cloud or cellular link. On a controlled greenhouse drought trial with wild radish, the fused model reached 87% accuracy (R^2=0.88, MAE=0.05) at 1.4 s INT8 TensorFlow Lite inference, and its soil signals preceded visible wilting by about four days. The complete bill of materials is $205, roughly a fifth of comparable commercial nodes, positioning multimodal, sustainable crop sensing as a practical consumer-electronics product for connectivity-limited settings.

title: Beyond Update Counts: A Control Map for Evaluating Test-Time Model Updates
abstract: Test-time updating lets a language model change persistent state after training---such as model weights, adapter parameters, or a memory module---before or while answering queries. Existing evaluations often compare systems using update count or frequency and performance measured immediately afterward. These summaries omit what is updated, where, when, and in what order. The same total can therefore hide an important difference: one system may answer after one update while another answers after two. We introduce the Control Map, an evaluation framework that records the committed updates preceding each scored answer and separately evaluates behavioral changes, immediate learning (acquisition), later recall (retention), preservation of unrelated behavior (locality), and performance in new settings. We prove when counts alone determine final state and show, under stated assumptions, how differences between pre-answer histories limit differences in average scores. Using ControlMap, our experiments reveal three insights. First, update scheduling matters: at a 760M-parameter checkpoint, 24 schedules with the same update count yield 19.7%--34.2% accuracy. Second, learning an edit does not guarantee that it lasts or remains contained: all six selected CounterFact LoRA settings learn the new information, while ROME retains edits at all 13 operating points but fails locality at each. Third, no editor performs best consistently across models, benchmarks, and tests. Evaluations should therefore report update histories and assess acquisition, retention, and locality separately.

title: SG-Splat: Stable Geometry Learning under Pose Uncertainty for Pose-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has become a promising representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. For practical deployment, recent studies have explored pose-free feed-forward 3DGS, which reconstructs Gaussian representations directly from unposed input images. However, these methods remain sensitive to residual pose errors, which perturb canonical-space Gaussian transformation, introducing noisy supervision for geometry and attribute learning. To address this problem, we present SG-Splat, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that improves robustness to pose uncertainty and stabilizes the learning of Gaussian primitives. SG-Splat decouples geometry estimation and Gaussian attribute prediction into two dedicated branches, reducing error coupling between pose-sensitive geometry and Gaussian attributes. We further introduce a coarse-to-fine refinement pipeline, consisting of Flow-Guided Pose Refinement (FGPR) and Residual-Guided Geometry Correction (RGC), to improve geometric alignment before Gaussian attribute reconstruction. Specifically, FGPR refines camera poses with flow-based correlation features and differentiable bundle adjustment. RGC then corrects initial point maps using depth residuals derived from FGPR, producing more reliable Gaussian centers. To stabilize training, we introduce a dual-path strategy that mixes ground-truth and predicted poses for canonical transformation. It provides clean supervision for Gaussian attributes while improving geometry robustness to residual pose errors. Extensive experiments on DL3DV and RealEstate10K show that SG-Splat achieves state-of-the-art performance in both novel view synthesis and pose estimation.

title: Useful Diversity or Hallucinated Variety? Persona-Conditioned Synthetic Query Generation for E-Commerce Search
abstract: Synthetic supervision can bootstrap semantic parsers in new search domains, but prompt-induced diversity is useful only when generations are faithful to the structured intent. We explore this for cold-start e-commerce search: 118,098 synthetic pairs produced by 6 LLMs with 9 persona-conditioned prompt families on a 47-field UK automotive schema, against 1,214 human-annotated and 15,304 production queries. We show that the IPIP personality bundle improves parser F1 in all four matched contrasts (Holm-corrected $p<.001$), and all three bundles have a positive main effect over the complete $2^3$ grid. Syntax conditioning is the axis that moves generations towards real traffic. It also induces lexical diversity. Alignment sKL, the divergence between von Mises-Fisher distributions fitted to synthetic and human-annotated queries, is an unlabelled proxy for parser F1 ($ρ=-0.917$ against human queries written for simulated shopper scenarios, lower is closer). An LLM committee, checked against a blinded author pass, triages the 927 queries missed by every parser and labels 37% as hallucinated. Dropped constraints dominate. The four syntax-bearing families have the largest hallucinated shares, 38 to 42%, while IPIP alone has the lowest at 28%.

title: Semantic Atoms for Scalable Text Analysis in Data Analytics in the Era of LLM-Based Agents
abstract: Much of the information needed for data analysis is buried in text columns: an analyst may infer customer frustration from complaint text and use it to explain resolution time. We call workloads in which processing text columns is central to subsequent data analysis TADA (\emph{Text Analysis in Data Analytics}). In an agentic setting, the user's query dynamically specifies this processing, and answering it interleaves LLM-based semantic steps with exact SQL or Python operations. This mixed execution raises two design questions: which work should be neural and which symbolic, and which semantic outputs later steps can reuse. We address them for agent-planned TADA workflows with two complementary, query-driven semantic atoms. Each atom takes a sequence of text items and a natural-language query specifying the semantic task: \textbf{Tagging} returns one string per input item, while \textbf{Categorization} returns $M$ category objects over $N$ input items. Tagging results are materialized as a row-aligned column and Categorization results as a category table; SQL or Python then performs exact computation over this exposed state. We realize this interface in TADA-Agent, whose atoms run inside generated Python programs and internally handle inputs beyond a reliable context window. We evaluate TADA-Agent on TABench, a benchmark of 40 complete analysis requests over spreadsheet tables spanning workflow composition, input--output structure, and literature-grounded analytical scenarios. Against a semantic-operator baseline and relative to a held-out TADA reference run, TADA-Agent delivers comparable row-level semantic quality, has higher complete-artifact preservation estimates, and uses over an order of magnitude fewer semantic-model requests under the evaluated native execution paths.

title: Nonlinear coupling between motional modes in trapped-ion quantum processors
abstract: Trapped-ion crystals are a leading platform for quantum information science, but achieving the high-fidelity entangling gates required for fault-tolerant quantum computing becomes harder as system size increases. As systems scale, spectral crowding makes low-order nonlinear resonances between collective motional modes increasingly common and can limit gate performance, especially in monolithic or global-mode architectures. We develop a general model to identify and simulate nonlinear motional-mode coupling (NoMoCou) arising from third-order Coulomb terms and quantify its impact on the Molmer-Sorensen gate across linear chains and 2D crystals in rf and Penning traps. We delineate the regimes where NoMoCou dominates the error budget and provide design rules: detune operating points from low-order resonances, tune trap anisotropy to reshape spectra, and shape gate waveforms.

title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol
abstract: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. We operationalize the injected directive through Trigger, Tool Binding, Justification, and Pressure, and separately measure call success, payload fidelity, and preservation of legitimate behavior. We evaluate five MCP servers and four LLM agents using five metrics spanning effectiveness, utility, and efficiency. Across 18 model-server pairs with valid tool execution, Log-To-Leak achieves an attack success rate (ASR) of 62.64-100% and conditional logging accuracy (LA) of 76.55-95.64%; 16 pairs have absolute target-task completion changes of at most 6.63 percentage points. Three evaluated defenses leave residual ASR above 55% on GitHub MCP with GPT-4o, while an instruction detector flags 85.53% of benign descriptions. These results show that successful task completion can coexist with unauthorized post-hoc disclosure and motivate host-controlled authorization for secondary tool calls.

title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
abstract: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because errors of fitted Q-functions and occupancy-ratio estimates cannot be directly evaluated from held-out transitions. Bellman-residual and minimax validation methods often require auxiliary regressions or optimization over separate critic classes, adding computational and tuning costs. We introduce pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a tuning-free minimax procedure for selecting among finite classes of fitted Q-functions and occupancy-ratio estimators using held-out transitions. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, requiring only finitely many empirical moment calculations without auxiliary validation models or separate critic optimization. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. Our key insight is that Q-function errors and log ratios between candidate and true occupancy ratios provide oracle critics whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Pairwise candidate differences approximate these unknown critics, while penalties account for comparator approximation error. For Q-function selection, we first develop unweighted PBV, which evaluates pairwise Bellman moments under the offline distribution and admits oracle guarantees under a pairwise coercivity condition relating the offline distribution to the target-policy dynamics. We then develop target-aligned PBV (TA-PBV), which uses marginalized importance weighting to provide error control without pairwise coercivity. For occupancy-ratio selection, we develop adjoint PBV (A-PBV), which evaluates adjoint Bellman moments against log-ratio critics. On Hopper and Deep OPE, unweighted PBV performs competitively, while target-occupancy weighting can improve performance in settings with controlled overlap.

evidence.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Bellman Tournaments
evidence.abstract: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because estimation errors in fitted $Q$-functions and occupancy ratios cannot be directly evaluated using held-out transition data. Existing Bellman-residual-based validation methods often require auxiliary regressions, while many minimax-based methods require optimization over separate critic classes. We propose pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods that reduces validation to computing held-out sample averages. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, on the log scale for occupancy ratios, and selects the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score. This construction approximates oracle critics given by $Q$-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios, whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. For $Q$-function selection, unweighted PBV avoids importance weighting but requires a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. Importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV) uses marginalized importance weighting to exploit Bellman contraction under the target-policy occupancy measure, avoiding this condition. For occupancy-ratio selection, adjoint PBV (A-PBV) exploits KL contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator to obtain oracle guarantees under the offline data law. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.

title: Adapt for Planning, Not just Prediction: Optimistic Test-Time World Model Adaptation
abstract: Latent world models are typically pre-trained offline and kept frozen at test time, so planning with them can degrade under distribution shift. Test-time adaptation (TTA) can mitigate this degradation by updating the model during deployment. Unlike pre-training on fixed data, TTA for planning is closed-loop: the planner uses model rollouts to select actions, and the resulting transitions drive the next update. This raises the question: which objective should guide TTA for planning? Under a prediction-only objective, the model is fit only to the outcomes of its own actions, so it can remain wrong about the actions that would reach the goal, and low prediction error need not translate into better planning. Inspired by reward-biased maximum likelihood from adaptive control, we introduce Optimistic Test-Time Adaptation (OpTTA). Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.

Its objective has two terms, the prediction loss on observed transitions and the planner's goal-reaching cost on its candidate rollouts, both minimized over the model parameters. The planning term biases adaptation toward models that are optimistic about reaching the goal, without any additional environment interaction. Across visual and environment shifts on manipulation, reaching and navigation tasks, OpTTA raises final planning success over the frozen model by 13.5 percentage points on average, compared with 6.9 for the prediction-only objective (AdaJEPA), when only the predictor is adapted. When the encoder is adapted as well, the gains are 13.5 and 7.5 points. These experiments span three JEPA world models with different encoders and training objectives and, for temporal straightening, both CEM and gradient-based planners. Our results suggest that test-time adaptation of world models for planning benefits from an optimistic, task-aware term in addition to the prediction loss.

title: Agreement Between Reconstructed and Native GDELT GKG Records: A Field-Level Baseline
abstract: The Global Knowledge Graph (GKG) of the Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone (GDELT) characterizes news articles using named entities, topics, quantitative and temporal features, quotations, tone, and dictionary-based content measures. Its codebook defines the record format, but the software that produces the records is not public, so researchers cannot generate compatible records for articles they collect themselves. We built an open-source reconstruction, gdelt-regkg, and measured how closely it agrees with GDELT's archived (native) records for 193,550 English articles from 8,729 publishers (2020-2025) and 2,500 articles in five other languages. Agreement depends strongly on the field. English tone, the percentage of positive minus negative words, has a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.79 points and a concordance correlation coefficient of 0.75. Identity agreement (F1) is 0.65 for persons, 0.42 for organizations, and 0.65 for locations. It is lower for date components (0.42), complete counts with their objects and locations (0.07), and quotations (0.07), while GCAM category presence reaches micro F1 0.84 within the implemented dictionaries. In subsets where retrieved and native titles and lengths match, tone error falls to 1.47 and organization F1 rises to 0.48, yet most disagreement remains. A larger gazetteer raises coverage of native places from 89.5% to 97.1% with little change in location F1. Tone computed on English translations of non-English articles is less accurate (MAE 2.10-2.64) than for English articles. The results are conditional on article pages that could still be retrieved, and the correspondence subsets do not isolate the effect of input differences. Reconstructed records should therefore be assessed field by field and not treated as completely interchangeable with native ones.

title: Spherical Brownian Diffusion for Language Modeling
abstract: Continuous diffusion language models involve two coupled design choices: how to corrupt continuous token representations and how to invert that corruption at generation time. Recent work has explored language generation on the unit sphere through geodesic and von Mises--Fisher (vMF) paths, raising the question of which forward process to use on this geometry and how much that choice matters relative to inference. We introduce Spherical Brownian Diffusion, using Brownian motion as the canonical isotropic diffusion on the sphere. Its heat semigroup provides a principled forward process, an additive dimension-free noise clock, and an exact ancestral bridge, while a clean-token posterior learned with cross-entropy supports multiple samplers. To separate corruption from inference, we derive high-dimensional approximation rates between Brownian and moment-matched vMF corruption and use this relationship for controlled substitutions. On Sudoku, Brownian and moment-matched vMF give nearly identical results across four samplers and five budgets under otherwise identical settings. In contrast, with the corruption process fixed, sampler choice produces a 25.0-point spread at a sampler budget of 180 calls. Using the ancestral bridge, we split this gain into a memory effect from re-noising the state, present on Sudoku and GSM8K, and a token-selection effect on GSM8K and largest at small budgets. Across reasoning tasks, categorical refinement improves performance, whereas unconditional text generation benefits from stochastic updates that preserve diversity.

title: DecoyCount: Evaluating Visual-Reasoning Misalignment in Counting
abstract: Visual counting benchmarks report whether vision-language models produce the correct number, but not whether errors arise from perception or reasoning. We introduce DecoyCount, a benchmark built from 1,586 real-world images with designed decoys across seven mechanisms, along with paired prompts: a neutral question, a matched alignment cue, and a novel multi-hop, multi-image question that situates the same counting problem in a realistic scenario. Using this design, we find that counting failures are induced partly by visual misalignment: models can execute the intended counting process when cue-guided but fail to select it unaided, and we term this difference in accuracy the reasoning-alignment gap. Despite being highly capable on general reasoning, frontier models remain below 50% accuracy on our benchmark, while alignment gaps range from 12.1-22.1 percentage points; strikingly, we observe that more capable models, greater thinking budgets, and agentic processes often induce larger gaps. Because humans may bring context that models lack, we test whether textual underspecification contributes to misalignment using a scenario-based multi-hop condition without explicit hinting, but this added context does not improve aggregate performance. Our analysis concludes that stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning, leaving misalignment with human visual expectations as a substantial component of the remaining deficit. DecoyCount and the evaluation code are released at https://github.com/elorian-ai/decoycount.

title: A general approach to permutation polynomials from quadratic forms
abstract: We investigate a family of polynomials over finite fields of characteristic 2 related to quadratic forms, and present a general treatment to study permutation properties of those polynomials. By determining some character sums associated with quadratic forms, we explicitly describe several classes of permutation polynomials.

title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.

title: SEMA-Auto: Sighted and Efficient Multi-Turn Attack with Autonomy
abstract: Existing jailbreak attackers fall into two classes: static planners fix their single- or multi-turn adversarial plans in advance, remaining simple but losing sight of the victim's replies, wasting turns and limiting transferability; interactive generators read each victim reply to generate the next-turn attack but require in-loop evaluators for success signals or hints, incurring substantial costs and inflated performance. Bridging this gap, we propose SEMA-Auto, a sighted and efficient multi-turn attacker with autonomy, interacting with the victim model and terminating the session by itself upon success. To stabilize its behaviors and boost its capabilities, SEMA-Auto is trained in two stages. Synthetic bootstrap tuning installs the notion of attack targets and conforming decisions by fine-tuning the base model with bootstrapped trajectories. Decision-supervised reinforcement learning then optimizes two objectives jointly yet separately, reinforcing the attack with higher jailbreak reward while supervising the decision at each turn against an absolute target. Our method achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) attack success rates (ASR) across multiple datasets, victims, and judges, outperforming all static and interactive baselines, within almost the fewest turns, demonstrating both effectiveness and efficiency. For example, SEMA-Auto performs a $76.0\%$ ASR@1 within an average of $3.0$ turns against DeepSeek-V4-Flash on AdvBench, while the best static baseline is $54.8\%$ with fixed $7$ turns and the best interactive baseline is $43.8\%$ in $3.7$ turns. Against safety-hardened frontier models, GPT-oss-120B, GPT-5.4, Claude-Haiku-4.5, and GPT-6-Astra, our counter-trained attacker achieves an average $59.6\%$ ASR@1 on HarmBench, $13.8\%$ over prior SOTA. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/SEMA

title: Offline Language-Based Support System for Tactical Decision-Making in Air Combat Operations
abstract: An offline language-based support tool is presented to assist pilot training and tactical decision-making in air combat operations. The system, named MATE (Mission Assistant for Training and Evaluation), applies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to answer natural language questions using content extracted from doctrinal and tactical manuals. Built entirely with open-source components, it performs text preprocessing, embedding generation, semantic search, and language generation locally, ensuring full offline functionality. The tool was evaluated by three Brazilian Air Force fighter pilots, who rated the answers produced with three open-weight language models (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 14B, and Mistral NeMo 12B) to five tactical questions derived from a publicly available air combat manual. Average ratings ranged from 4.00 to 4.40 on a five-point scale, with Mistral NeMo 12B obtaining the highest score, and the pilots rated the response time of the tool as fully adequate compared to manual search. The relevance of the retrieved content was identified as the main point for improvement. Potential applications are discussed in onboard mission systems, flight simulators, and training environments.

title: Benchmarking uncertainty quantification for engineering regression under graded distribution shift
abstract: Machine learning models in engineering are often used beyond their training conditions, where reliable uncertainty quantification (UQ) matters most. Existing comparisons of regression UQ methods rely on random splits, which assess calibration only in distribution. We introduce a three-rung shift ladder (in distribution, soft shift and hard shift) built along physically meaningful shift variables, and evaluate 12 methods from five families on seven public engineering datasets: five extrapolation settings, an unseen turbofan fault mode and a winter air-quality sensor deployment. All tuning uses source data only. In distribution, conformal methods cover at least 0.946 of test points on every dataset. Under hard shift, mean coverage falls to 0.40-0.75 across the 11 methods that always return an interval, and no systematic difference in method ranks is detected (Friedman p = 0.63). Weighted conformalised quantile regression stays near nominal on the points it answers, but abstains on 85\% of hard-shift points on average and covers only 0.67 of the few Concrete points it answers. Source-validation gains predict improvement in distribution and under soft shift, but not under hard shift (Spearman's rho = 0.04). Engineering evaluations should split calibration data by deployment unit, report subgroup coverage and sharpness, and treat abstention as an explicit operational outcome.

title: RAGing Against Misogyny: Improving Implicit Misogyny Explanations
abstract: Implicit misogyny often requires background knowledge to be understood. To address this challenge, we propose a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for detecting and explaining implicit misogyny in English and Italian, leveraging encyclopedic, slang and feminist knowledge sources. Using the ImplicIT-Mis and SBIC+ datasets, we evaluate the contribution of each knowledge source to detection and explanation quality, investigating also whether RAG addresses known LLM failure modes in implicit misogyny. Results show that RAG improves recall on ImplicIT-Mis, but does not improve detection performance on SBIC+. However, human evaluation shows that RAG-based explanations are preferred over no-RAG explanations in both languages. Feminist literature emerges as the most consistently useful source for detection and explanation.

title: Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Bounds for Online Linear Optimisation on $\ell_p$ Balls
abstract: We study full-information online linear optimisation on the unit $\ell_p$ ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, for fixed $2\le p<\infty$ and losses of dual norm at most one. Let $Δ_T$ denote the cumulative loss of the best fixed action above each round's minimum. A follow-the-regularised-leader (FTRL) algorithm attains, on every loss sequence and without knowing $T$ or $Δ_T$, regret $O_p(1+\min\{Δ_T^{1-1/p},\, d^{1/2-1/p}\sqrt{Δ_T}\})$. Matching lower bounds show that this rate is minimax for each fixed $p$, and its constant $(2+o(1))p/\log p$ is optimal as $p\to\infty$ among guarantees uniform in $d$ and $T$. The algorithm uses a bounded radial regulariser and switches at most once to its quadratic augmentation. On some paths where follow-the-leader (FTL) has regret one, its regret grows with $T$. A switching extension keeps the sharp constant and also guarantees $\mathrm{Reg}_T\le 2\,\mathrm{Reg}_T^{\mathrm{FTL}}$. For i.i.d. losses whose mean has no zero coordinates, we compute the exact $\log T$ coefficient of the expected regret, which separates FTL's variance term from the bias of the regulariser.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
abstract: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.

title: OneEEG: A Unified Signal-Visual Multimodal Language Model with Task-Aware Mixture of Projectors for Multi-Task EEG Understanding
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in clinical assessment, brain-computer interfaces, and cognitive-state analysis, yet EEG modeling remains fragmented across task paradigms. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a promising interface for flexible multimodal reasoning, but their ability to understand EEG inputs remains limited. In this work, we propose OneEEG, a unified EEG-MLLM framework for multi-task EEG understanding. By training on our curated OneEEG-Instruct, a multi-task EEG instruction-tuning dataset, OneEEG jointly models numerical EEG representations and visual EEG representations, and introduces a task-aware Mixture of Projectors (MoP) to align heterogeneous EEG features across different task families with the LLM embedding space. We further establish OneEEG-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating current MLLMs and our method on multi-task EEG understanding. Experiments show that existing MLLMs have limited ability to interpret EEG inputs, while OneEEG achieves stronger performance by integrating numerical and visual EEG representations with task-aware EEG-to-LLM projection. Extensive ablations and analyses further reveal the effects of visual EEG renderings, MoP variants, router behavior, and feature dispersion across EEG tasks.

title: Improving Instruction Hierarchy by Learning from Goal-Goal Conflicts
abstract: The recent incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously compromised Hugging Face's infrastructure illustrates the importance of instruction hierarchy (IH): an LLM should follow lower-priority instructions, such as user requests, only when they do not conflict with higher-priority instructions, such as system policies. IH can be effectively improved by fine-tuning LLMs on simulated examples of instruction conflicts, whose diversity is key to teaching LLMs to properly handle conflicts at test time. However, our decomposition of a task into goals and constraints reveals a conflict type -- goal-goal conflicts -- that is absent from existing IH training sets from OpenAI and NVIDIA. We show the importance of this conflict type: fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B-it on examples of this conflict type significantly improves IH on a wide range of real-world tasks unseen in training; adding these examples to existing IH training sets for fine-tuning also gives better IH adherence. The IH gains come with trivial mean utility changes on no-conflict tasks across eight benchmarks. Our work advocates including this new conflict type in IH training, even if these examples do not reflect typical LLM use.

title: Recovering Black-Box Point Cloud Models from Pose Shifts via Derivative-Free Optimization
abstract: Point cloud models are increasingly deployed through score-only black-box interfaces. Under this access model, test-time rotations outside the training distribution can substantially degrade performance. Although existing mitigations such as equivariant retraining and gradient-based adaptation are effective, they are infeasible without access to model weights or gradients. To address this limitation, we propose CanDO, a test-time canonicalization method that recovers lost performance using only forward queries. Specifically, CanDO searches for an input transformation that maximizes model confidence and uses derivative-free optimization to perform this search without gradients. We further identify three conditions for successful recovery: a training augmentation gap, an accuracy-aligned confidence surrogate, and global search over a multi-modal objective. Across multiple architectures and benchmarks, CanDO recovers 76% of the oracle gap under azimuthal misorientation and 51% under arbitrary SO(3) rotations for object part segmentation. These results show that frozen score-only point cloud models can recover from rotation-induced distribution shifts through post-deployment canonicalization alone.

title: Real-time detection of correlated quasiparticle tunneling events in a multi-qubit superconducting device
abstract: Quasiparticle tunneling events are a source of decoherence and correlated errors in superconducting circuits. Understanding and ultimately mitigating these errors calls for real-time detection of quasiparticle tunneling events on individual devices. In this work, we simultaneously detect quasiparticle tunneling events in two co-housed, charge-sensitive transmons coupled to a common waveguide. We measure background quasiparticle tunneling rates at the single-hertz level, with temporal resolution of tens of microseconds. Using time-tagged coincidence analysis, we show that individual events are uncorrelated across devices, whereas burst episodes occur about once per minute and are largely correlated. These bursts have a characteristic lifetime of 7 ms and induce a thousand-fold increase in the quasiparticle tunneling rate across both devices. In addition, we identify a rarer subset of bursts which are accompanied by a shift in the offset charge, at approximately one event per hour. Our results establish a practical and extensible method to identify quasiparticle bursts in superconducting circuits, as well as their correlations and spatial structure, advancing routes to suppress correlated errors in superconducting quantum processors.

title: SpeeDiff: Scalable Pixel-Anchored End-to-End Latent Diffusion Model
abstract: We present Scalable Pixel-anchored End-to-end Diffusion (SpeeDiff), a latent diffusion method that jointly trains the VAE and the diffusion model from scratch. In principle, joint training allows the diffusion loss gradient to directly guide the VAE encoder, encouraging the formation of a generation-friendly latent space and potentially yielding faster convergence than the conventional two-stage approach with a pretrained frozen VAE. However, a naive end-to-end implementation severely degrades performance, as unrestricted backpropagation of the diffusion loss leads to latent space collapse. Our main technical contribution is a simple yet effective Tweedie Pixel Reconstruction (TPR) loss, which provides additional pixel-level feedback by decoding a predicted clean latent from an intermediate noisy state using Tweedie's formula, thereby alleviating collapse. Furthermore, our method enables jointly scaling a fully transformer-based architecture and enhances representation alignment within the end-to-end framework. Our SpeeDiff-XL model achieves over 140x and 61x faster training compared to Vanilla SiT and REPA, respectively, while attaining an FID of 1.50 without guidance on ImageNet 256x256 generation. With a more efficient 32x compressed VAE, our model further reaches an FID of 1.53 without guidance on ImageNet 512x512 generation.

title: Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
abstract: An adversary brain is an LLM-based model of a threat actor's behavior, held as an evolving logical signature: a hypothesis with enough structure that data can test it continuously, without a person re-interpreting it each time. Rather than any single observation, such as an IoC (Indicator of Compromise), it is the arrangement that becomes a detection, or intelligence, mechanism. Where YARA matches a file and Sigma matches a log line, an adversary brain matches the activity pattern of a campaign or threat actor. This is based on an intelligence analysis technique called Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH), which the design lifts from the limitation of a few hypotheses at a time, to thousands, and then also operationalizes it for continuous detection purposes. Language models make the concept, and scale, practical: they turn prose reports into brains, judge matches, and drive the loop that keeps brains current. A partial pattern in a brain can also match a new value, such as a fresh C2 (command and control) domain name, assisting with the discovery of new indicators, and turning unknown unknowns into known unknowns, and potentially into knowns. The author would like to thank Ryan Moon for the collaboration, and Sounil Yu, Chris Inglis, Thomas Roccia, Marius Benthin, Israel Grimberg, Michal Kamensky, Justin Borland, Brandon Levene, John Hultquist, and John Bambenek for their feedback and assistance.

title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation
abstract: Recent studies have applied large language model (LLM) agent systems to computational simulation workflows. Such workflows are long-horizon, so the information generated can exceed what an LLM can reason over at once, its context window. Context management is therefore essential, yet existing systems have either neglected it or treated it as a supporting mechanism rather than a subject of study. This paper presents MarkovSim, an LLM agent harness for long-horizon computational simulation, whose core is a context management scheme built into the workflow. The workflow record is written to a memory system with a predefined schema, and at workflow-defined boundaries, namely the state transitions of a finite-state machine a compact representation of the solution progress is constructed from it as the agent's context. Instantiated on finite element analysis and evaluated on six benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs and corrected its own faults in both the solver operations and the model physics. The engineer was consulted only where engineering judgement was needed. The context remained bounded throughout every run, regardless of its length.

title: Uncertainty Evaluation to Support Safety of the Intended Functionality Analysis for Determining the Applicability of Performance Targets Across Triggering Conditions in ML-Based LiDAR Object Detection
abstract: For safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) analysis according to ISO 21448, a machine learning object detector for light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds can meet a performance target, a limit on the mean per-frame share of wrong detections among accepted detections, by rejecting detections above an uncertainty threshold. A threshold selected on data of one condition carries a statistical guarantee only for data distributed like its selection data, whereas SOTIF analysis covers every triggering condition. This paper presents an uncertainty evaluation in which the threshold is transferred into a triggering condition, a test decides at a stated error probability whether the target is applicable there, not applicable or not determined, and a lower bound counts the independent units an applicable outcome requires. For PointPillars ensembles on KITTI and nuScenes, counted in recorded sequences, as the dependence between frames requires, neither dataset held enough independent units for any target limit, and no transfer had a not applicable outcome. Counted in frames, the same data gave not applicable outcomes at limits fixed in advance after transfers into far distance, into rain and between two separately trained detectors, thresholds that met the target limit after a transfer rejected most correct detections, and in rain the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve did not decrease. A performance target met under one condition therefore counts as evidence under a triggering condition only after a test there, reported with its share of accepted correct detections and its number of independent recorded sequences.

title: Seeing Before Naming: Context-Grounded Learning of Novel Visual Concepts
abstract: Learning an unfamiliar visual category requires more than adapting a classifier: the model must connect its visual evidence to a useful semantic name. A pre-trained vision-language model can retain discriminative image features while providing a weak textual anchor for the target concept. We address this imbalance through context-grounded semantic anchoring. Our framework, SynerNet, learns concept-specific name embeddings, exposes them to compatible linguistic contexts, and conditions their representations on visual evidence. Difficulty-aware processing and adaptive objective weighting coordinate this adaptation while retaining the pre-trained backbone. On four VISTA-Beyond domains, SynerNet reaches a mean 16-shot accuracy of 74.35%, compared with 72.45% for few-shot name learning. Across 14 domains in the name-masked transfer setting, it improves mean accuracy from 45.17% to 46.74%. Ablations identify concept-specific name embeddings and cross-modal context integration as important components. These results support treating concept acquisition as the construction of visually grounded semantic anchors.

title: A Practical Post-Quantum Distributed Ledger Protocol for Financial Institutions
abstract: Traditional financial institutions face inefficiencies that can be addressed by distributed ledger technology. However, a primary barrier to adoption is the privacy concerns surrounding publicly available transaction data. Existing private protocols for distributed ledger that focus on the RingCT model are not suitable for adoption for financial institutions. We propose a post-quantum, lattice-based transaction scheme for encrypted ledgers which better aligns with institutions' requirements for confidentiality and audit-ability. The construction leverages various zero-knowledge proof techniques, and introduces a new method for equating two commitment messages, without the capability to open one of the commitment during the re-commitment. Subsequently, we build a publicly verifiable transaction scheme that is efficient for single or multi-assets, by introducing a new compact range-proof. The techniques used and the proofs constructed could be of independent interest.

title: Verifiable Efficiency Limits of Innate LLM Planning in Sliding Puzzles
abstract: Tool-assisted planning success can reflect external search and verification, leaving a model's unaided planning ability unresolved. We isolate innate planning through complete plans generated in one response without tools or execution feedback. We propose a verifiable framework that decomposes success-weighted plan efficiency as $\mathrm{SPE}=R\times Q\times E$: execution reliability, planning coordination among legal plans, and action economy among completed plans. Trajectory replay and certified optima verify these factors; the joint score includes unsuccessful attempts. We evaluate 8,400 full-plan outputs from seven model conditions on $4\times4$ sliding puzzles, controlling exact horizon and obstacle count in the primary cohort. Models that complete every trial still become less economical at longer horizons, while higher efficiency among completed plans can coexist with poor goal attainment. SPE separates the overall capability hierarchy, while its factors distinguish coordination failure from inefficient completion. The framework makes long-horizon limitations in unaided planning quantitatively verifiable.

title: FinLLM-KG: Knowledge Graph-Enhanced LLMs for Financial Sentiment Analysis in Algorithmic Trading
abstract: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to predicting the sentiment of each article in isolation and operate as black boxes, which limits contextual understanding and hinders deployment in high-stakes financial decision-making. To this end, we introduce FinLLM-KG, a model-agnostic framework that combines causal LLMs with a financial knowledge graph, in order to inject temporally grounded, company-level knowledge from SEC 10-K filings at inference time, without updating model weights. Within FinLLM-KG, context is supplied either as a natural-language company profile or as a small set of relevance-ranked factual triples. This enables sentiment predictions to account for broader firm-level information rather than the article alone, at almost zero computational cost and for any causal LLM. In addition, attributing each article-level sentiment score to individual sentences and to the retrieved knowledge-graph facts makes the evidence behind the prediction inspectable, thereby enhancing explainability and supporting human-in-the-loop review. Simulations demonstrate that FinLLM-KG consistently improves portfolio performance over the state-of-the-art baseline.

title: CVTSplat: Multi-view Reconstruction Using an Adaptive Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation
abstract: Voronoi tessellations have recently emerged as an adaptive, space-partitioning discretization for shape and appearance reconstruction from multi-view images. However, the irregular cells they produce make the repeated reconstruction of the tessellation during optimization costly. We therefore explore adaptive centroidal Voronoi tessellations (CVTs), which extend standard CVTs with non-uniform cell sizes while preserving the regular, well-shaped cells that make them efficient to compute. In CVTSplat, cell size is modulated by the evolving signed distance field, concentrating sites near the zero level set while keeping cells nearly centroidal. This regularity lets us specialize the whole pipeline, with GPU algorithms for nearest-neighbor queries and approximate Voronoi construction, and a rasterizer tailored to small, nearly isotropic cells. Our Voronoi construction is 5 to 10 times faster than general-purpose alternatives in this regime. On DTU and BlendedMVS, CVTSplat reaches geometric accuracy competitive with the best Gaussian-splatting surface methods while training in about 2.5 minutes on a single GPU.

title: Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition
abstract: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.

title: PosePlaner: Denoising Any Feed-Forward Pose Predictor from Pairwise Planar Geometry
abstract: Recent multi-view Transformers (e.g., DUSt3R and VGGT) have advanced 3D reconstruction by scaling training data and model capacity from two views to many views and long sequences, subsuming the classical SfM/SLAM pipeline of feature extraction, matching, and pose estimation in a single feed-forward pass. Yet this subsumption hides the interfaces between pipeline stages---correspondences, geometry, and pose are entangled in a single forward pass, leaving supervised fine-tuning as the major path to improvement and offering no mechanism to correct predictions from geometric evidence at test time. We propose PosePlaner to close this gap by reviving the classical coupling between correspondences and pose via flow matching, treating pose refinement as a conditional generation problem that takes coarse geometric matches and initial pose as input condition and fuses the resulting pose hypotheses into a single refined estimate, providing a continuous, data-driven analog of RANSAC voting. Our method is trained efficiently on two-view data, yet serves as a periodic refiner for streaming n-view pose estimators with no retraining. Empirically, it corrects failures of feed-forward predictors, substantially improves correspondence-based solvers, and reduces accumulated drift in long streaming sequences.

title: Quantum protocols for time synchronisation and distribution: a critical assessment
abstract: Precise time synchronisation underpins critical infrastructure from telecommunications and financial markets to power grids and scientific metrology. Several families of quantum protocols have been proposed and demonstrated for clock synchronisation and time distribution, exploiting entangled photon pairs, quantum key distribution (QKD) correlations, Hong-Ou-Mandel interference, and entangled clock networks. We critically assess these approaches, reviewing the main quantum time synchronisation (QTS) protocol families, quantifying the gap between theory and experiment, and identifying practical bottlenecks in sources, detectors, and channels. We survey the classical timing landscape from Network Time Protocol (NTP) and GPS to laboratory-grade optical frequency transfer, and compare quantum and classical methods at equivalent maturity. We examine use cases including financial trading, power grids, telecommunications, scientific metrology, and military applications, evaluating whether quantum timing offers a realistic advantage. We show that time transfer, not clock performance, is now the bottleneck for distributed optical timekeeping: the best demonstrated quantum synchronisation uncertainty (2.46 ps, over 20 km of fibre) falls two to three orders of magnitude short of what optical clocks with fractional frequency uncertainties of 10 −18 –10 −19 require. The best deployed link, ELSTAB, calibrates to a few tens of picoseconds in the laboratory and to about 0.2 ns on its 421 km field installation, a further factor of twenty to a hundred behind, while research-grade classical links using optical frequency combs already reach the regime the clocks require, though none is in operational service. Our assessment is that quantum time synchronisation will not replace classical methods for most applications in the near-to-medium future, yet it can complement them. Its near-term value lies in physical-layer security against timing manipulation and integration with quantum communication networks, while closing the synchronisation gap for scientific metrology remains the most critical open challenge.

title: Coherent Ratios for Compositional Data Analysis with Zeros
abstract: Compositional data (CoDa) are scale-invariant by nature, and their analysis traditionally relies on log-ratio transformations. A cornerstone of the Aitchison school is the principle of subcompositional coherence: analyses should be consistent when focusing on any subset of parts, a property that follows from the isomorphism property of the logarithm. However, zeros in the data render log-ratio transformations undefined, posing a fundamental challenge. This paper introduces a family of transformations based on a ratio-based homeomorphism, which maps extended non-negative numbers to the unit interval. By applying it to suitable ratios of components, we construct both i) local representations that require a reference component (or a set of components) to be non-zero, and ii) global representations that handle zeros in all components simultaneously. We show that the local representations preserve subcompositional coherence for subcompositions containing the reference part, a property deemed essential by the log-ratio community, while the global representations trade this coherence for the ability to accommodate zeros everywhere. Thus, no single transformation satisfies all desirable properties, but the local approach offers a principled compromise: it retains subcompositional coherence and enables a quasi-global treatment of zeros. The practical utility of the approach is illustrated on a glass dataset for predicting the refractive index, where the proposed local representation outperforms standard log-ratio methods with zero imputation, matches industry benchmarks, and yields interpretable coefficients consistent with domain knowledge. The proposed framework provides a flexible, imputation-free toolbox for analyzing compositional data with zeros, allowing analysts to choose between coherence and full coverage depending on the application, and enabling the use of standard multivariate techniques on bounded, interpretable coordinates.

title: Persistence, Exposure, and Credit Routing in Linear Temporal Predictive Coding
abstract: Temporal Predictive Coding (tPC) networks offer a layer-local alternative to backpropagation. For linear tPC, we show, by applying tools from cellular sheaf theory, that temporal credit assignment is a tug-of-war between spatial displacement and temporal errors, whose ratios are modulated by persistence and exposure operators $P$ and $Q$. Spatial inference therefore gives us the effective recurrent transition $F=PA$, whilst future credit is filtered by $P^\ast$. This creates a persistence--error tradeoff in spatial modes: under non-amplifying invariant recurrence, modes that preserve influence over long delays simultaneously fail to expose that influence strongly as temporal error. Recurrence can circumvent this via routing between persistent and exposed modes.

title: Distilling neural networks into equations to predict planetary instability
abstract: The problem of predicting when a multi-planet system will become dynamically unstable has defied analytical progress over the past three hundred years. Recent machine learning advances achieve high predictive performance of instability dynamics, but as black-box systems cannot be interpreted to connect to existing scientific understanding. Here we show analytic equations that predict when a multi-planet system will undergo instability. We discover these equations by first training a neural network on a dataset of N-body simulations, and then distilling its latent knowledge into closed-form algebraic expressions. Our two-stage pipeline first learns an interpretable variable basis, then searches for equations using symbolic regression. The resulting equations outperform existing analytic estimates of instability and apply across wide ranges of mass ratios, spacing, and orbital eccentricities. They capture structure in the prediction landscape with a small number of variables amenable to dynamical interpretation. These results demonstrate how symbolic learning can be combined with neural networks to extract scientific insight from complex dynamical systems.

title: Should Pseudo-Labels Share Mini-Batches with Labeled Examples? Semi-Supervised Continual Active Learning with Limited Training Cost
abstract: Active learning (AL) reduces annotation by querying informative examples. Continual active learning (CAL) also cuts the training cost, the total number of gradient steps, by training one model across AL rounds with a fixed number of mini-batch steps per round. Pseudo-labels add supervision without annotation, but they increase training cost. In CAL, where every round trains on a fixed number of mini-batches, whether and how pseudo-labeled examples should share these mini-batches with labeled examples is therefore open. We provide the first formalization of this problem as two decisions after each query, namely (i) which unlabeled examples should enter training with a pseudo-label and (ii) what share of each mini-batch they should take. Our method, semi-supervised continual active learning (SSCAL), works with any acquisition function. It admits pseudo-labels based on distances from unlabeled examples to labeled neighbors, caps their share, and reweights the loss on labeled examples to keep their expected gradient contribution unchanged. On frozen embeddings, its pseudo-labeler updates incrementally without extra model forward passes. Across two audio datasets, two frozen encoders, six acquisition functions and ten seeds, SSCAL ranks first on average among four protocols with equal training steps, answering the question affirmatively.
